analyst:
Akron enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 28-6 overall after finishing the regular season 26-5 and 17-1 in the Mid-American Conference, then winning three straight games in Cleveland to claim the MAC automatic bid. The regular-season mark placed the Zips second in the MAC behind unbeaten Miami, and Akron’s 17-1 league finish gave John Groce’s program a 34-2 conference record across the last two seasons. In the MAC title game on March 15, 2026, Akron beat Miami 76-74 on Nate Johnson’s buzzer-beater with two seconds left, pushing the final record to 28-6 and giving the Zips a third straight MAC tournament championship. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Akron_Zips_men%27s_basketball_team))

Offensively, Akron is built like a modern spread-MAC attack but with very traditional guard decision-making. The numbers show the identity clearly: 89.6 points per game, a 124.3 offensive rating, 50.3% team field-goal shooting, and 37.9% from three over 34 games. Akron’s own game notes also documented that by early January the Zips ranked third nationally in assist-turnover ratio, sixth in assists per game, third in scoring offense, tenth in effective field-goal percentage, and 27th in fast-break points. That profile matches what shows up on film and in recaps: five-out spacing, heavy drive-and-kick action from Tavari Johnson, second-side ball movement, and a willingness to use the bench as an extension of the offense rather than a changeup. Akron is 12-2 when making at least 10 threes, and under Groce the Zips are 100-22 when they hit that threshold. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/akron/men/2026-schedule.html?utm_source=openai))

Specific tendencies matter here. Akron repeatedly wins games with avalanche runs created by spread pick-and-roll and quick extra-pass threes. In the 104-89 win over Western Michigan on January 17, the Zips tied the program record with 20 made threes and flipped the game with a 13-0 second-half burst after trailing 58-52; Shammah Scott scored 23 off the bench and Bowen Hardman hit 4-of-6 from deep. Against Ohio on January 23, Akron used a 16-0 first-half run to build a 48-26 halftime lead in an 86-65 road win, and the bench supplied 28 points. Against Northern Illinois on March 6, Akron made 18 threes in a 94-55 blowout. Those are not random hot nights; they reflect a designed offense that prioritizes paint touch to kick-out, trail threes in transition, and volume spacing around Johnson and the Mahaffey frontcourt. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-akron-shoots-57-1-percent-from-deep-beats-western-michigan-104-89?utm_source=openai))

Akron’s half-court structure also leans on multiple handlers instead of one dominant table-setter. Tavari Johnson averages 20.1 points and 5.0 assists, while the team averages 18.4 assists per game. Amani Lyles gives them a scoring wing/forward at 14.6 points and 8.0 rebounds per game, and the Mahaffey brothers add connective passing and interior finishing. Evan Mahaffey averages 10.2 points, 5.6 rebounds, and 3.5 assists, which is important because Akron often plays through elbows and short-roll reads rather than pure post-ups. The statistical spread across the top seven scorers supports that balance: Johnson 20.1, Lyles 14.6, Scott 12.7, Evan Mahaffey 10.2, Bowen Hardman 7.9, Eric Mahaffey 7.8, and Sharron Young 7.3 points per game. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2006))

Defensively, Groce’s team is not an elite shutdown unit possession for possession, but it is a very specific one. Akron forces mistakes, runs shooters off rhythm, and then turns live-ball stops into offense. By early January the Zips ranked 21st nationally in turnover margin and 54th in turnovers forced per game. In the 69-52 home win over Kent State on January 30, Akron held the Golden Flashes to 28.4% overall and just 1-for-23 from three, while forcing 15 turnovers. In the 86-65 win at Ohio, Akron held the Bobcats to 32.8% from the field and 23.5% from three. In the March 3 win at Central Michigan, Akron forced 17 turnovers. The philosophy is more contain-and-swarm than pure gambling: limit clean catch-and-shoot looks, pressure the first pass, and let activity from guards and mobile forwards create rushed possessions late in the clock. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/5/mens-basketball-akron-hosts-central-michigan-on-tuesday?utm_source=openai))

Groce’s coaching philosophy shows up in documented game-to-game and in-game adjustments. He is comfortable changing the scoring source without changing the structure. When Western Michigan led by six in the second half on January 17, Akron answered not with isolation but with a 13-0 run fueled by perimeter volume and bench scoring. When Kent State threatened to make the January 30 game a possession game, Akron doubled down on spacing and kept generating three-point looks, finishing with 11 made threes and 17 assists. When Miami beat Akron 76-73 on January 3, the Zips still got four double-figure scorers and a 10-point, 13-rebound double-double from Eric Mahaffey, but the result exposed that Akron can be vulnerable when a disciplined opponent keeps it out of rhythm late. The strongest evidence of Groce’s adjustment history came in the rematch: on March 15 in the MAC championship, Akron beat that same Miami team 76-74 on a final-possession winner by Nate Johnson, showing a clear ability to recalibrate after the regular-season loss. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-akron-shoots-57-1-percent-from-deep-beats-western-michigan-104-89?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is good enough to trust because there are named examples. The biggest one is March 15, 2026: Akron 76, Miami 74, with Nate Johnson hitting the game-winner with two seconds left to send the Zips to the NCAA Tournament. Another is January 3, 2026, when Akron lost at Miami 76-73; that game matters because it showed the Zips could generate enough late offense to stay even with the league’s best regular-season team but did not finish the final possessions. A third is the January 17 comeback against Western Michigan: Akron trailed 58-52 before a 13-0 run turned control of the game. A fourth is the January 30 Kent State game, where Akron never trailed and effectively executed the closer’s script by stretching the margin from 38-29 at the half to a 17-point final. Akron’s late-game profile is therefore less about grinding out many one-possession games and more about using shotmaking spurts to seize control before the final minute, then having Johnson available when a true final shot is needed. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Akron_Zips_men%27s_basketball_team))

The key players start with Tavari Johnson, the engine. He averages 20.1 points, 5.0 assists, shoots 51.2% from the floor, 37.3% from three, and 87.0% at the line. His best single-game scoring example is 35 points against Yale on November 24 in a 97-94 loss in the Paradise Jam title game. That game also highlighted Akron’s offensive ceiling against strong competition, because Shammah Scott added a career-high 25. Johnson also had 22 points in the MAC title win over Miami and 22 in the January 3 loss at Miami, reinforcing that he is the primary late-clock creator. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2006))

Amani Lyles is the second pillar, averaging 14.6 points and 8.0 rebounds on 55.7% shooting and 37.5% from three. Recent form matters: on January 23, the Akron recap noted he had scored in double figures in 15 straight games and had double-doubles in consecutive outings. He is the piece that prevents Akron from being too guard-dependent because he can score as a mismatch forward, rebound traffic, and still space the floor. Shammah Scott, at 12.7 points per game and 42.2% from three, is the premium bench weapon; his 23 points against Western Michigan and 25 against Yale show true swing-man impact. Evan Mahaffey is a glue forward who averages 10.2 points, 5.6 rebounds, and 3.5 assists, while Eric Mahaffey gives Akron interior activity and rebounding, including a 10-point, 13-rebound double-double at Miami. Hardman is the specialist shooter: 7.9 points per game, 40.7% from three, and 15 points with five made threes against Kent State on January 30. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2006))

Akron’s notable wins reveal a team that can overwhelm peers when the ball moves. The March 15 MAC final win over Miami, 76-74, proved composure against the league’s best regular-season team. The January 30 69-52 win over Kent State revealed defensive discipline and rivalry-game control; holding a rival to 1-of-23 from three is a real tournament-quality indicator. The January 23 road win at Ohio, 86-65, showed travel-proof offense and defense together. The January 17 win over Western Michigan, 104-89, showed comeback capacity and nuclear three-point variance in Akron’s favor. The March 6 Senior Day destruction of Northern Illinois, 94-55, showed how dangerous the Zips are when role players are making shots in volume. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Akron_Zips_men%27s_basketball_team))

The notable losses are just as instructive. The January 3 loss at Miami, 76-73, showed that Akron can be bothered by a disciplined opponent that survives its scoring balance. The November 24 Yale loss, 97-94, showed a defensive ceiling issue against an efficient, experienced offense even when Johnson and Scott combined for 60 points. Ball State also beat Akron 70-63 on January 6, a result Akron’s own game preview referenced later in the month; that game is a reminder that when Akron’s perimeter rhythm dips, the offense can become more ordinary. Those losses do not erase the ceiling, but they define the upset path: make the Zips defend multiple actions cleanly, survive Johnson’s creation, and keep them below the 10-made-three benchmark. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-akron-falls-76-73-to-miami-oh?utm_source=openai))

As for Groce’s NCAA tournament history, it is substantial and relevant. At Ohio, he led NCAA trips in 2010 and 2012; the 2012 Bobcats reached the Sweet 16 after beating Michigan and South Florida before losing to North Carolina in overtime. At Illinois, Groce reached the 2013 NCAA Tournament and advanced to the Round of 32. At Akron, he has taken the Zips to the NCAA Tournament in 2022, 2024, 2025, and now 2026, with first-round appearances in 2022 against UCLA and 2024 against Creighton documented in his Akron bio. In total, his head-coaching tournament résumé includes a Sweet 16 at Ohio in 2012, a Round of 32 at Illinois in 2013, and four NCAA bids at Akron including this 2026 berth. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/john-groce/1154?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Akron is not just a “good MAC team.” It is a 28-6 league champion with a top-end offense, a deep scoring rotation, a lead guard in Tavari Johnson who has both 35-point firepower and game-winner credibility, and a coach in John Groce with real March history. The swing question against high-major opposition is whether Akron’s defense can survive when the threes are merely average rather than overwhelming. But if the Zips get into their preferred game — spread floor, quick decisions, bench shotmaking, and run-producing defense — they are capable of making a favored seed play deep into the second half. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Akron_Zips_men%27s_basketball_team))

Akron enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the more interesting profile splits in the field: a mid-major with elite raw offensive production, strong predictive efficiency in some systems, but a résumé ceiling capped by schedule quality and a lack of high-end wins. As of games through March 15, 2026, Akron is 27-5 against Division I opponents, 17-1 in the MAC, and sits at No. 54 in the NCAA NET. WarrenNolan’s team sheet lists Akron’s predictive ranks at No. 77 in ESPN BPI, No. 64 in KenPom/POM, and No. 71 in Bart Torvik’s T-Rank, while also showing a very weak NET strength of schedule at No. 241 and non-conference NET SOS at No. 234. In quadrant terms, that résumé is thin at the top: 0-2 in Q1, 0-2 in Q2, 11-1 in Q3, and 16-0 in Q4. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Akron))

The headline number is the offense. WarrenNolan’s 2026 advanced team stats place Akron eighth nationally in offensive rating at 123.2 points per 100 possessions. The same source has the Zips at a defensive rating of 104.5, yielding a net rating of +18.7, which ranks 14th nationally. That is a remarkable predictive signal for a team seeded and résumé-slotted more like a lower-end at-large or strong automatic qualifier than a top-15 efficiency team. Sports-Reference’s season summary aligns with that broad picture, listing Akron at 124.3 points scored per 100 possessions and 102.2 allowed, with 89.6 points per game scored and a simple rating system mark of 9.76. Across sources, the precise defensive figure varies somewhat, but the core conclusion is stable: Akron is an offense-first team with national-top-10 scoring efficiency and defense that is materially better than its points-allowed-per-game reputation suggests once tempo is considered. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating?utm_source=openai))

Tempo is central to understanding Akron. WarrenNolan lists the Zips at 71.4 possessions per 40 minutes, one of the faster paces in Division I. That pace helps explain why the team’s raw scoring numbers are gaudy and why its raw defensive numbers can look ordinary: Akron plays more possessions than most of the country, so both points scored and points allowed are inflated in counting terms. Sports-Reference likewise shows 89.6 points per game, sixth nationally, while WarrenNolan lists 75.7 points allowed per game, only around the middle of the pack. The possession-adjusted view is much kinder. This is not a lockdown defense, but it is also not the weak unit casual observers might infer from a 75.7 points-allowed figure. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-pace?utm_source=openai))

Stylistically, Akron’s offensive engine appears to be driven by shotmaking and second chances more than foul pressure. NCAA team stats had Akron at 50.43% overall field-goal percentage through mid-February, ranking 15th nationally at that checkpoint. WarrenNolan’s offensive rebounding percentage for Akron is 33.9%, an excellent figure and a major driver of extra possessions. By contrast, Akron’s free-throw attempt rate is just 0.294, tied down at No. 321 nationally, indicating this is not a team that consistently manufactures offense by living at the line. That low foul-drawing rate is a meaningful vulnerability in tournament settings, because it reduces floor-raising easy points when perimeter shooting cools. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/stats/basketball-men/d1/current/team/148?utm_source=openai))

Ball security looks solid-to-good rather than elite. WarrenNolan lists Akron at 11.0 turnovers per game, tied around 106th nationally. That is consistent with a high-powered offense that usually gets to a shot and does not waste too many possessions, though it does not by itself establish an elite turnover percentage. The available public data I could verify gives stronger support to Akron’s offensive rebounding profile and scoring efficiency than to a precise team TO%. So the cleanest read is that Akron’s attack is powered primarily by efficient shooting and possession extension on the offensive glass, with acceptable ball care and relatively modest free-throw generation. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-off-to-per-game?utm_source=openai))

On the résumé side, conventional wisdom and the metrics diverge sharply. Conventional selection logic sees a team with a NET in the mid-50s, a BPI in the high 70s, no Q1 wins, no Q2 wins, and a schedule ranked outside the top 230. Predictive efficiency, however, sees something stronger: KenPom 64, Torvik 71, and WarrenNolan net rating 14th nationally. That is the profile of a dangerous tournament offense hidden inside a modest résumé shell. The explanation is straightforward: Akron crushed a lot of weaker competition, did so efficiently, and avoided bad losses more than it stacked marquee wins. The team sheet shows losses to Purdue on the road, Miami (OH) on the road, Yale on a neutral floor, and Troy on the road, with a road-heavy record of 9-3 overall and 7-4 in non-conference play. So this is not purely a home-track bully, but neither is it battle-tested against the top two quadrants. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Akron))

Recent form is strong if you look at outcomes. Akron closed the MAC season and tournament with wins over Buffalo, Kent State, and Toledo on a neutral floor, and the team sheet shows a March 12-14 run beating Buffalo 73-70, Kent State 75-68, and Toledo 79-76. That supports the idea that the Zips entered the NCAA field in good competitive shape. I could not verify a clean publicly available exact “last 10 games efficiency” table for Akron from a primary source accessible here, but the outcome trend is clearly positive and consistent with a team that sustained top-end offense into March. Given their season-long offensive rating and late neutral-floor wins, the best synthesis is that Akron’s offense remained the carrying force over the final stretch, while the defense held just enough for MAC-level control. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Akron))

The eye-test contradiction is this: Akron may look like a classic fun-but-flawed mid-major because the games are fast, the scores are huge, and the defense can appear loose. The numbers say that read is too shallow. This is not merely a hot-shooting upset dart; it is a legitimately elite offensive efficiency team with strong offensive rebounding, real pace pressure, and enough defensive competence to finish with a top-15 net rating in one public efficiency system. The counterargument is equally real: weak schedule strength, poor foul-drawing, and an absence of quality-win proof against Q1/Q2 competition. Put together, Akron profiles as a team more dangerous than its seed line or conventional résumé scan would imply, but also one whose margin for error narrows quickly if the jump shooting normalizes and the whistle is tight. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-net-rating?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Akron enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as an offense-first team built around pace, spacing, and ball movement. Through 34 games, the Zips averaged 88.4 points per game, shot 50.3% from the field, 37.9% from three, and posted an estimated 123.1 offensive rating using season totals from Akron’s cumulative stats. Their estimated pace is about 71.0 possessions per game, which is fast by NCAA standards. They also averaged 18.4 assists against 10.9 turnovers, and Akron was 10-0 when reaching 20 assists, a strong indicator that their best offense is collective rather than isolation-driven. Tavari Johnson is the engine at 20.1 points and 5.0 assists per game, with Amani Lyles at 14.6 points and 8.1 rebounds, Shammah Scott at 12.7 points, Evan Mahaffey at 10.2 points and 3.5 assists, and Bowen Hardman adding 77 made threes on 40.7% shooting from deep. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The style is clear: Akron wants to score early, spray the ball to multiple shooters, and force help decisions. In late November, Akron ranked 29th nationally in fastbreak points at 19.5 per game, 6th in assists per game at 21.1, and 16th in threes attempted per game at 32.5. By mid-January, they still ranked 19th nationally in fastbreak points at 16.32 per game, 3rd in scoring offense at 93.6, and 3rd in effective field-goal percentage at .607. That profile fits what the film and box scores show: Johnson collapses the defense, Scott and Hardman punish tags, and Lyles can score as a stretch-4/inside finisher. The best disruption tactics are therefore specific: pick Johnson up early, switch or top-lock Scott and Hardman off flare actions, and force Akron into late-clock creation instead of first-action drive-kick basketball. The strongest evidence is Akron’s own win/loss split on ball movement: 10-0 when they get 20+ assists, meaning opponents have to turn them into a lower-assist, more individual offense. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-zips-travel-to-buffalo-on-tuesday))

Akron is much more team-offense than pure isolation offense. Their season totals show 627 assists on 1,090 made field goals, meaning 57.5% of all made baskets were assisted. Johnson alone created 170 assists, Evan Mahaffey added 118, Scott 100, and Lyles 74. By contrast, the highest-usage self-creators are Johnson and Scott, but even those two function mostly within spread pick-and-roll and kick-out sequences, not endless mismatch hunting. A practical reading: if you can flatten their assist chain and make Johnson score 1-on-1 over length, you at least move Akron away from the version that statistically wins most cleanly. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Press vulnerability is not severe in raw turnover rate terms, because Akron’s assist-turnover ratio was elite all year and they averaged only 10.9 turnovers per game. Still, pressure can bother specific lineups because the primary small-guard creator is Tavari Johnson at 5-11, and the rotation relies heavily on guards under 6-3: Johnson 5-11, Sharron Young 6-0, Scott 6-2, Hardman 6-3. If you can trap Johnson and deny easy reversal entries, Akron’s size thins out in the backcourt. That said, the counterexample is strong: against Western Michigan on January 17, Akron shredded a game with 23 assists and just enough control to turn it into a 104-89 win while making 20 threes; against Buffalo on January 20, Johnson had 32 points and eight assists in a 90-58 road win previewed in Akron’s game notes; and for the full season the Zips ranked top-15 nationally in assist-turnover ratio. So the right takeaway is not “full-court press them every possession,” but “use selective dead-ball pressure and aggressive half-court traps at Johnson to burn clock and force secondary initiators.” ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-zips-travel-to-buffalo-on-tuesday))

Zone is the more interesting question. Akron’s shooting makes lazy zone dangerous: they made 371 threes as a team, and six players had at least 20 made threes by late February. They tied the school record with 20 threes against Western Michigan, made 18 threes against NIU in a 94-55 win on March 6, and hit 11 threes against UMass in a 99-92 win while also scoring 26 fastbreak points and 24 points off turnovers. But zone can still work if it is long and active enough to take away rhythm catch-and-shoot looks and force Akron to finish over size inside. Akron’s forwards are skilled, but not overwhelming vertical lob threats. Against Troy on February 7, Akron lost 79-69 despite Johnson scoring 26; the rest of the main rotation was much more ordinary, with Lyles scoring 9, Scott 11, Young 3, and the team losing the physical battle to a longer, stronger Sun Belt opponent. That game is useful evidence that athletic length and bodying the wings can push Akron off its ideal shot diet. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2026/2/6/Akron_Notes.pdf))

Preferred pace is fast. Their estimated season pace sits around 71 possessions, and all of Akron’s cleanest offensive explosions came in games played in the 90-point range: 104-89 over Western Michigan, 99-92 over UMass, 99-85 over Buffalo, 96-75 over Iona, and 94-55 over NIU. To force the opposite, you must make them defend multiple actions in the half court, limit live-ball turnovers, and send two hard sprint-backs to the arc in transition. In the UMass game, Akron generated 26 fastbreak points and 24 points off turnovers; that is the exact category to kill if you want to drag them into a 66-possession grinder. Conversely, Yale beat them 97-94 even while Akron shot 52.2% from three, which suggests Akron can be hurt when opponents score efficiently enough to negate the Zips’ spacing advantage and keep them from setting the terms. Troy did it more physically; Yale did it by matching shotmaking and offensive efficiency. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/umass/boxscore/11014))

Position-by-position mismatch notes matter. At point guard, Johnson is dynamic but small at 5-11; bigger guards can shoot over him or post him after switches. At the two/three, Scott (6-2), Young (6-0), and Hardman (6-3) can all be shot-targeted defensively against bigger wings, though Hardman’s spacing is critical offensively. At the four, Lyles is productive at 6-7/6-9 listing range depending on source, but power-conference length can test him as a rim finisher and defensive rebounder. At the hybrid forward spot, Evan Mahaffey is Akron’s best all-around athlete and connective piece at 6-6; he had 57 steals and 26 blocks, so teams need to know he is their best playmaker on the back line defensively. Eric Mahaffey gives them more size on the glass, but Akron overall is still not huge by NCAA Tournament standards. The likely mismatch target is Akron’s small backcourt, especially if an opponent has 6-4 to 6-6 wings who can both switch onto Johnson and finish over Young/Scott. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/akron/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Transition offense frequency is clearly a major part of the identity, with nationally ranked fastbreak scoring in multiple checkpoints: 19.5 per game in late November and 16.32 per game in mid-January. Transition defense is more mixed. Akron forced 14.33 turnovers per game by mid-January and finished with 256 steals over 34 games, so they often create transition by defense. But when opponents survive the first wave, Akron’s defense is only good rather than dominant: opponents still shot 42.2% overall and made 311 threes, and Akron’s estimated defensive rating was about 102.3. UMass scored 92 on them, Yale scored 97, Troy scored 79 in a slower game, Toledo scored 81 despite Akron’s comeback win, and Buffalo put 85 on the board in late February. That is evidence that Akron can be scored on by teams with enough shotmaking and enough discipline to avoid feeding its runout game. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-zips-travel-to-buffalo-on-tuesday))

Coaching adaptability under John Groce is a real strength. Akron’s January 27 win over Toledo is the clearest example: the Zips trailed 49-41 at halftime, then opened the second half on an 8-0 run and won the half 50-32 to take a 91-81 win. That is concrete halftime adjustment evidence, not theory. Groce’s team also responded after the Troy loss by beating UMass 99-92 with 37 bench points, 26 fastbreak points, and balanced scoring. More broadly, Akron has sustained elite home performance under Groce and a long stretch of offensive continuity, suggesting a stable identity with counters rather than a one-note scheme. The one limit on “mid-series” evidence is structural: college basketball does not play playoff series, so the best available adjustment evidence is game-to-game and halftime response, where Akron grades well. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/27/mens-basketball-akron-secures-91-81-win-against-toledo-after-trailing-at-the-half?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Akron, you must first eliminate live-ball mistakes and transition threes. Second, put a long defender on Tavari Johnson and trap him selectively after the first ball screen; make Scott, Young, or Evan Mahaffey initiate late in the clock. Third, switch or top-lock Hardman and Scott off movement so the pass count drops; remember Akron is undefeated when it reaches 20 assists. Fourth, play a long matchup zone or switchable man that runs shooters off the line but still bodies Lyles on the glass. Fifth, attack Akron’s small guards with size every trip, especially in cross-matches. Sixth, make it a half-court possession game: 65-67 possessions is the target, not 72+. If Akron gets comfortable in spread transition and drive-kick rhythm, they can score 90 on anybody in their league context; if you make Johnson work over length, deny the kick-out chain, and turn it into a physical half-court game like Troy did, you give yourself the best path to beat them. ([gozips.com](https://gozips.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-zips-travel-to-buffalo-on-tuesday))
